text: Woe unto them that are mighty to drink wine, and men of strength to mingle strong drink…
reflection: Isaiah pronounces a series of woes on the people of his day, and one of them is surprisingly pointed: "Woe unto them that are mighty to drink wine, and men of strength to mingle strong drink." These people were proud of a kind of strength, but it was strength spent in the wrong place. They could drink more than anyone, yet they had no strength to do justice or resist corruption. The next verse says they took bribes and denied justice to the innocent. It is a sobering reminder that not all strength is true strength. We can be strong in ways that do not matter and weak in ways that do. We can boast about endurance in pleasures while lacking the courage to do what is right. As we begin this month on courage and strength, ask God to redirect your strength. Where are you spending your energy? Real strength is found in standing for what is good, protecting the vulnerable, and walking in integrity. That kind of strength comes from God.
question: Where are you spending your strength, and how could it be redirected toward what is good?
prayer: Lord, keep me from wasting my strength in the wrong places. Turn my energy toward justice, integrity, and protecting the vulnerable, with strength that comes from You. Amen.

text: Saying, We give thee thanks, O Lord God Almighty, which art, and wast, and art to come; because thou hast taken to thee thy great power, and hast reigned.
reflection: In John's vision, the elders in heaven fall on their faces and worship: "We give thee thanks, O Lord God Almighty, which art, and wast, and art to come; because thou hast taken to thee thy great power, and hast reigned." This is a song of victory. God has taken His great power and begun to reign openly over all things. Notice how they describe Him: the One who is, who was, and who is to come. He has always been present, He is present now, and He will be present forever. His power is not a passing season of strength. It is eternal. When we feel weak, this vision reminds us who is ultimately in control. Kingdoms rise and fall, but God remains Almighty. Every power that resists Him will eventually bow. And His people respond not with fear but with thanksgiving. Today, give thanks to the Lord God Almighty. Whatever feels out of control in your life, remember that He reigns, and His power is greater than anything you face.
question: What feels out of control in your life that you can thank God for reigning over?
prayer: Lord God Almighty, You are, You were, and You are to come. I give You thanks that You reign over all, even over what feels out of control in my life. Amen.

text: And they were all amazed at the mighty power of God. But while they wondered every one at all things which Jesus did, he said unto his disciples…
reflection: Jesus had just healed a boy whom the disciples could not help. The crowd was astonished: "And they were all amazed at the mighty power of God." Everyone marveled at what Jesus had done. But in that very moment, Jesus turned to His disciples and spoke about His coming suffering. While the crowd was focused on spectacular power, Jesus pointed to the cross. That is significant. God's mighty power is displayed in miracles, yes. But it is displayed most fully in the cross and resurrection, in self-giving love that conquers sin and death. The disciples wanted a powerful Messiah who would only win. They struggled to understand a Messiah who would suffer. Yet the power of God is perfected in weakness. Today, marvel at the mighty power of God. But also remember that His power often works in ways we do not expect: through humility, sacrifice, and love. Trust His strength, even when it looks different from what you imagined.
question: Where might God's power be working through humility or sacrifice in a way you did not expect?
prayer: Lord Jesus, I am amazed at Your mighty power. Help me trust Your strength even when it works through humility, sacrifice, and love rather than what I expected. Amen.

text: Through mighty signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God; so that from Jerusalem, and round about unto Illyricum, I have fully preached the gospel of Christ.
reflection: Looking back on years of ministry, Paul was careful to give credit where it was due. Everything had been accomplished "Through mighty signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God." He had traveled across vast regions preaching the gospel, but he knew it was not by his own strength. The Spirit had done the work. This is a freeing truth. We are not called to accomplish God's purposes in our own power. We are called to depend on His Spirit. Paul was gifted, determined, and hardworking, but he never confused his effort with God's power. Perhaps you are facing a task that feels too big for you. A calling, a responsibility, a challenge that stretches you beyond your ability. Remember that the same Spirit who empowered Paul is available to you. You do not have to do it alone. Today, invite the Spirit to work through you. Offer your effort, but trust His power. Then give Him the credit.
question: What task can you invite the Spirit to empower today, giving Him the credit afterward?
prayer: Holy Spirit, I cannot accomplish Your purposes in my own power. Work through my effort today, and let all the credit go to You. Amen.

text: (For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
reflection: Paul reminds us that the battles we face are not fought with ordinary weapons: "For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds." A stronghold is a fortified place, hard to break down. In our lives, strongholds can be patterns of thinking, deep fears, lies we believe, or habits that seem impossible to overcome. We often try to fight them with willpower or human strategies, and we grow discouraged when they do not budge. But Paul says our weapons are mighty through God. Prayer, Scripture, truth, faith, and the power of the Spirit can tear down what human strength cannot. This does not mean the battle is instant or easy. Strongholds may come down brick by brick. But they can come down. Today, identify one stronghold in your life. Bring it before God in prayer. Speak His truth over it. Trust that the weapons He gives are strong enough to bring it down.
question: What stronghold in your life can you bring before God in prayer and speak His truth over?
prayer: Lord, the weapons You give are mighty to pull down strongholds. I bring You the fears, lies, and habits that hold me, and I trust Your truth to bring them down. Amen.

text: And I heard a loud voice saying in heaven, Now is come salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ: for the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night.
reflection: John heard a loud voice in heaven announcing victory: "Now is come salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ: for the accuser of our brethren is cast down." The accuser is the enemy who constantly points out our failures, day and night. He whispers that we are not good enough, that God could never love us, that our past disqualifies us. But heaven declares that the accuser has been cast down. Through the blood of Jesus, his accusations no longer have power over God's people. This is where true strength comes from. Not from proving ourselves innocent, but from trusting the One who has defeated the accuser. When guilt and shame rise up in your mind, remember this verse. The voice of accusation has been overruled by the verdict of grace. Salvation and strength have come. Today, stand in the victory of Christ. Refuse to listen to the accuser. You are forgiven, and you are free.
question: What accusation do you keep listening to that Christ's victory has already overruled?
prayer: Lord Jesus, the accuser has been cast down by Your victory. When old accusations rise, help me stand in Your grace, knowing I am forgiven and free. Amen.

text: Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high…
reflection: Hebrews opens with a majestic description of Jesus: He is "the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power." Jesus shows us exactly what God is like. He is not a faint reflection but the radiance of God's glory. And He is not distant from creation. He holds it all together by His word. Every star, every breath, every heartbeat is sustained by Him. Then the verse continues: "when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high." The King who holds the universe together also stooped to cleanse us from sin. And having finished that work, He sat down, the posture of a King whose work is complete. This is our promised King. He is powerful enough to uphold all things and humble enough to save us. Today, rest in Him. The One holding the universe is also holding you.
question: How does it steady you to know that the One upholding all things is also holding you?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the brightness of God's glory and uphold all things by Your word. You have purged my sins and sit enthroned on high. I rest in You today. Amen.

text: Who is this King of glory? The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle.
reflection: Psalm 24 imagines a procession approaching the gates of Jerusalem. A question rings out: "Who is this King of glory?" And the answer thunders back: "The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle." This is the God we serve. He is not weak, distant, or easily defeated. He is strong and mighty, a warrior King who fights for His people. When we face battles, whether in our health, our relationships, our work, or our own hearts, we do not face them alone. The LORD mighty in battle goes before us. This does not mean every struggle ends the way we want. But it does mean we never fight without a powerful defender. Our courage does not come from our own strength. It comes from knowing who stands with us. Today, whatever battle you face, lift up your head. Open the gates of your heart and welcome the King of glory. He is strong, He is mighty, and He fights for you.
question: What battle are you facing today that you can welcome the King of glory into?
prayer: Lord, strong and mighty, mighty in battle, You fight for Your people. I lift up my head and open the gates of my heart to You, my King of glory. Amen.

text: And Jesus answering said unto them, Do ye not therefore err, because ye know not the scriptures, neither the power of God?
reflection: Some religious leaders who did not believe in the resurrection came to Jesus with a tricky question about marriage in the afterlife. Jesus answered them directly: "Do ye not therefore err, because ye know not the scriptures, neither the power of God?" Their mistake had two roots. They did not truly understand Scripture, and they underestimated God's power. They imagined God was limited by the same rules that limit us. But God is the God of the living. He raises the dead. He hears and answers in ways that exceed our imagination. We can make the same mistake. When we face impossible situations, we may assume God cannot do anything because we cannot see how. But Jesus calls us to know both the Scriptures and the power of God. When you pray, you are speaking to the One who raises the dead. Today, do not limit Him. Bring your impossible situations to the God who hears, and trust His power.
question: What impossible situation are you tempted to limit God in?
prayer: Lord, You are the God of the living and You raise the dead. Keep me from underestimating You, and help me bring every impossible situation to You in faith. Amen.

text: These have one mind, and shall give their power and strength unto the beast.
reflection: In Revelation's vision, a group of rulers make a fateful decision: "These have one mind, and shall give their power and strength unto the beast." They united, but in the wrong cause. They handed over their power to something opposed to God. The very next verse tells us how it ends: they make war with the Lamb, and the Lamb overcomes them, for He is Lord of lords and King of kings. This vision raises a question for each of us. To whom are we giving our strength? Our time, energy, talents, and influence are all forms of power. We can give them to things that serve God's purposes, or to things that oppose them. Sometimes we hand our strength over without even realizing it, to fear, to anger, to destructive habits, to causes that lead away from God. Today, consider where your strength is going. Choose to give it to the Lamb who conquers. His kingdom is the one that will stand.
question: To whom or what are you giving your strength, and is it leading toward the Lamb or away from Him?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are King of kings and Lord of lords. Keep me from giving my strength to what opposes You, and help me give it wholly to You. Amen.

text: Say to them that are of a fearful heart, Be strong, fear not: behold, your God will come with vengeance, even God with a recompence; he will come and save you.
reflection: Isaiah gives us a message to share with anxious people: "Say to them that are of a fearful heart, Be strong, fear not: behold, your God will come." Notice that this is a message to be spoken. We are called not only to receive courage but to pass it on. And the courage is not based on positive thinking or circumstances. It is based on God's coming. He will come and save you. The surrounding chapter describes the desert blooming, the blind seeing, the lame leaping. When God comes, everything changes. If your heart is fearful today, hear these words for yourself. Be strong. Fear not. Your God will come. He has not forgotten you. He will act on your behalf. And then think of someone else who is anxious. Perhaps a friend facing a diagnosis, a family member struggling with uncertainty, or a neighbor carrying a heavy burden. Speak these words to them. Your encouragement, rooted in God's promise, may be the courage they need.
question: Who around you has a fearful heart and needs to hear, "Be strong, fear not"?
prayer: Lord, You will come and save Your people. Strengthen my fearful heart, and give me words of courage for someone who needs to hear Your promise today. Amen.

text: Jesus answered and said unto them, Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God.
reflection: Matthew records the same encounter we saw earlier in Mark, but with a slightly different emphasis: "Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God." Jesus says it plainly: these leaders are in error. Their confusion was not harmless. It kept them from seeing God rightly and from hoping in the resurrection. Here, we are invited to consider how knowing Scripture shapes our prayers. When we know God's Word, we know His promises. We learn what He is like, what He has done, and what He has promised to do. That knowledge fuels confident prayer. We pray not into the void, but to a God who has revealed Himself. And when we know His power, we pray with expectation. Today, combine both. Open the Scriptures and find a promise to hold on to. Then bring it to God in prayer, trusting His power to fulfill it. A God who hears is also a God who is able to act.
question: What promise in Scripture can you hold on to and bring to God in prayer today?
prayer: Lord, teach me to know Your Scriptures and Your power. Help me find Your promises in Your Word, and pray them back to You with faith and expectation. Amen.

text: A wise man scaleth the city of the mighty, and casteth down the strength of the confidence thereof.
reflection: Proverbs paints a picture of a battle: "A wise man scaleth the city of the mighty, and casteth down the strength of the confidence thereof." A city full of warriors trusts in its walls and soldiers. But a wise person finds a way over the walls and topples the very thing the city relied on. The lesson is clear: wisdom is more powerful than brute strength. Throughout Scripture, God often uses the wise and humble to overcome the proud and mighty. A shepherd boy defeats a giant. A small band of soldiers routs a great army. What looks impressive in human terms is not always what wins. This is encouraging for anyone who feels small or outmatched. You may not have the most resources, influence, or physical strength. But wisdom from God can accomplish what force cannot. Today, when you face a challenge that feels too big, ask God for wisdom rather than more muscle. His insight can scale walls you thought were impossible.
question: What challenge seems too big, and how might wisdom from God help where force cannot?
prayer: Lord, Your wisdom is greater than any strength. When I face walls that seem too high, give me Your insight to find the way through. Amen.

text: Whereas angels, which are greater in power and might, bring not railing accusation against them before the Lord.
reflection: Peter describes false teachers who were arrogant and quick to insult those in authority. Then he contrasts them with the angels: "Whereas angels, which are greater in power and might, bring not railing accusation against them before the Lord." The angels, though far more powerful, refuse to use insulting, contemptuous speech. They leave judgment to God. This verse reveals a kind of courage that is often overlooked. It takes strength to restrain your tongue. It takes courage to disagree without mocking, to stand for truth without slander. In a world where harsh words and insults are everywhere, especially online, this is a needed lesson. Courage does not mean being loud or cutting. True strength can be gentle and controlled. Today, as you face disagreements or frustrations, follow the example of the angels. Speak truth, but speak it with respect. Leave judgment to God. Your restraint will reflect a strength far greater than any insult.
question: In a disagreement today, how can you speak truth with respect and leave judgment to God?
prayer: Lord, give me the strength of restraint. When I am frustrated, help me speak truth with respect, and leave judgment in Your hands. Amen.

text: Be thou exalted, LORD, in thine own strength: so will we sing and praise thy power.
reflection: Psalm 21 celebrates God's victories on behalf of the king, and it ends with a burst of praise: "Be thou exalted, LORD, in thine own strength: so will we sing and praise thy power." Notice where the focus lands. Not on the king's achievements, not on the army's success, but on God's own strength. The people recognized that every victory came from Him. So they lifted Him up and sang of His power. When good things happen in our lives, it is tempting to take the credit. When we overcome a challenge, we may admire our own resilience. But this psalm invites us to redirect our praise. God's strength made the difference. Exalting Him keeps us humble and grateful. And there is joy in it. Singing of God's power reminds us that we serve a mighty God who can be trusted in future battles too. Today, think of a recent victory or answered prayer. Give God the glory. Sing, speak, or write your praise for His strength.
question: What recent victory or answered prayer can you give God the glory for today?
prayer: Lord, be exalted in Your own strength. Every victory in my life comes from You. I will sing and praise Your power. Amen.

text: In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when ye are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ…
reflection: Paul writes to the Corinthian church about a serious problem: a member was living in open sin, and the church was ignoring it. Paul instructs them to act "In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when ye are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ." This was not about harsh punishment. Paul's goal, as he explains, was that the person's spirit might be saved. Church discipline, done rightly, is an act of love aimed at restoration. And it is carried out in the name and power of Jesus, not in human pride or anger. This verse reminds us that the church gathers under the authority of Christ. We do not have the strength to confront sin or restore the broken on our own. We need His power and His heart. Today, if you know someone who has drifted into harmful patterns, pray for them. Ask Jesus for wisdom and courage to speak lovingly, with restoration as the goal.
question: Who has drifted into harmful patterns that you could pray for and speak to with restoration in mind?
prayer: Lord Jesus, give me Your power and Your heart for those who have drifted. Help me pray for them faithfully and speak with love, aiming always for restoration. Amen.

text: Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away.
reflection: Paul describes people in the last days who are "Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away." They looked religious on the outside. They used the right words and kept up appearances. But they rejected the power that truly changes lives. Their faith was a shell, an empty form without the transforming work of God. It is possible to have religion without relationship, routine without reality. We can attend services, say prayers, and speak the language of faith while keeping God at arm's length. Paul's warning invites us to examine our own hearts. Is our faith only a form, or is it alive with God's power? The power of godliness is seen in changed lives: growing love, real repentance, and increasing joy. Today, ask God to make your faith real and alive. Invite His Spirit to work in the areas where you have been going through the motions. Do not settle for the form; seek the power.
question: Where have you been going through the motions of faith without seeking God's power?
prayer: Lord, I do not want the form of godliness without the power. Make my faith real and alive, and let Your Spirit work where I have been going through the motions. Amen.

text: Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time…
reflection: Peter offers a surprising path to strength: "Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time." We usually think strength means asserting ourselves, pushing forward, fighting for our place. But Peter says the way up is down. Humble yourself. Place yourself under God's mighty hand. Trust Him to lift you up when the time is right. That mighty hand is both powerful and caring. In the very next verse, Peter adds, "casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you." Humility is not thinking poorly of ourselves. It is trusting God enough to stop striving and let Him lead. It means waiting for His timing rather than forcing our own. This can feel vulnerable, but it is actually the strongest place to be. Under God's hand, we are protected and held. Today, humble yourself before Him. Release your need to control the outcome. Trust His mighty hand to lift you up in due time.
question: What outcome do you need to release as you humble yourself under God's mighty hand?
prayer: Lord, I humble myself under Your mighty hand. I release my need to control the outcome, and I trust You to lift me up in due time. Amen.

text: But, lo, he speaketh boldly, and they say nothing unto him. Do the rulers know indeed that this is the very Christ?
reflection: Jesus was teaching openly in the temple during a festival, even though the authorities wanted to arrest Him. The crowd was amazed: "But, lo, he speaketh boldly, and they say nothing unto him. Do the rulers know indeed that this is the very Christ?" People were wondering who Jesus really was. His boldness, wisdom, and authority made them ask whether He might be the promised Messiah. Jesus did not hide. He did not soften His message out of fear. He spoke the truth openly, because He was who He claimed to be. This question still echoes today. Is Jesus truly the Christ, the promised Savior? Many people are still wondering. The answer of the Gospels is a resounding yes. He is the One God promised, the Savior of the world. Today, consider your own answer to that question. And if you know Him, follow His example. Speak about Him with quiet boldness. Others may be wondering, just like that crowd.
question: Who do you say Jesus is, and how can you speak of Him with quiet boldness today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the Christ, the Savior of the world. Give me Your quiet boldness to speak about You to those who are still wondering. Amen.

text: Behold, we count them happy which endure. Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy.
reflection: James encourages believers who are suffering to take the long view: "Behold, we count them happy which endure. Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy." Job lost nearly everything, yet he endured. And in the end, God restored him and revealed His heart. That is the point James wants us to see. The end of the Lord, His ultimate purpose, is full of compassion. He is very pitiful, which means deeply tender, and full of mercy. On this Father's Day, this verse offers a beautiful picture of God as a compassionate Father. Even when we do not understand our suffering, His heart toward us is tender. Earthly fathers vary. Some are a blessing, others have caused pain. But your heavenly Father is perfect in mercy. Today, thank God for His tender compassion. And if you are a father or father figure, ask Him to help you reflect His gentle heart.
question: What hardship are you enduring, and how does God's tender mercy give you hope for the end?
prayer: Father, You are full of compassion and tender mercy. Help me endure as Job did, trusting Your good end. Bless every father, and help us reflect Your gentle heart. Amen.

text: Joseph of Arimathaea, an honourable counsellor, which also waited for the kingdom of God, came, and went in boldly unto Pilate, and craved the body of Jesus.
reflection: After Jesus died, His body hung on the cross while most of His followers had scattered. Then a surprising man stepped forward: "Joseph of Arimathaea, an honourable counsellor, which also waited for the kingdom of God, came, and went in boldly unto Pilate, and craved the body of Jesus." Joseph was a respected member of the council, a man with much to lose. Until then, he had been a quiet follower. But in that dark hour, he found courage. He went boldly to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus, risking his reputation and position. He gave the Savior an honorable burial in his own tomb. Joseph's story shows that it is never too late to step forward in faith. Some of us have been quiet believers, keeping our faith hidden. But there comes a moment when love for Jesus calls for courage. Today, ask God for the boldness of Joseph. Do one thing that honors Jesus openly, even if it costs you something.
question: What is one thing you could do today that honors Jesus openly, even if it costs you something?
prayer: Lord Jesus, give me the boldness of Joseph of Arimathea. When love for You calls for courage, help me honor You openly, whatever it costs. Amen.

text: Saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing.
reflection: In heaven, countless voices join in a mighty chorus: "Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing." Seven gifts are offered to the Lamb, a picture of complete and perfect praise. And notice the one being honored: a Lamb that was slain. Not a lion, not a mighty warrior, but a Lamb who gave Himself. In the kingdom of God, the highest honor goes to self-giving love. Jesus is worthy of all power and strength precisely because He laid down His life for us. This reshapes how we think about strength. True strength is not domination; it is sacrifice. And everything we have, our abilities, resources, and energy, can be offered back to Him as worship. Today, join the song of heaven. Tell Jesus that He is worthy. Then offer Him your strength as an act of praise, using it to serve, love, and honor Him.
question: How could you offer your strength to Jesus as an act of worship today?
prayer: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain! Lord Jesus, I give You my praise, and I offer You my strength to serve, to love, and to honor You today. Amen.

text: And with great power gave the apostles witness of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus: and great grace was upon them all.
reflection: In the early days of the church, something remarkable was happening: "And with great power gave the apostles witness of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus: and great grace was upon them all." Great power and great grace, side by side. The apostles spoke about the risen Jesus with boldness and conviction. And grace rested on the whole community. The surrounding verses describe believers sharing their possessions so that no one was in need. Grace was not only a spiritual idea; it showed up in generosity, unity, and care. This is what a grace-filled community looks like. It is bold in proclaiming Jesus and tender in caring for one another. Both power and grace come from God, and both are needed. Today, ask God to fill you with both. Speak about Jesus with confidence when the opportunity comes. And look for a practical way to show grace to someone in need. Where great grace rests, people are cared for and Jesus is made known.
question: Where can you speak about the risen Jesus with confidence, or show grace to someone in need?
prayer: Lord, let great power and great grace rest on me. Give me boldness to witness to Your resurrection, and help me care practically for someone in need. Amen.

text: Whereof I was made a minister, according to the gift of the grace of God given unto me by the effectual working of his power.
reflection: Paul marveled that God had called him into ministry. He wrote, "Whereof I was made a minister, according to the gift of the grace of God given unto me by the effectual working of his power." Paul did not appoint himself. He did not earn his calling. It was a gift of grace. And it was sustained by God's power working effectively in him. Remember, Paul had once persecuted the church. He considered himself the least of all believers. Yet God's grace made him a minister of the gospel. This is good news for anyone who feels unqualified for what God has called them to do. Your calling, whatever it is, is not based on your worthiness but on God's grace. And the power to carry it out is not your own. It is His power, working in you. Today, whatever responsibilities God has given you, at home, at work, at church, receive them as gifts of grace. Then lean on His power to fulfill them.
question: What responsibility can you receive as a gift of grace and fulfill by leaning on God's power?
prayer: Lord, every calling I have is a gift of Your grace. Help me receive my responsibilities with gratitude, and fulfill them by the working of Your power. Amen.

text: I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.
reflection: This is one of the most quoted verses in the Bible: "I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me." But its context gives it even deeper meaning. Paul was not talking about achieving every ambition or winning every competition. He was talking about contentment. He had learned to be content in poverty and in plenty, hungry or full. Whatever his circumstances, Christ gave him the strength to endure with peace. That is the true power of this verse. It is not a promise that we will always succeed. It is a promise that, whatever comes, Christ will strengthen us to face it faithfully. In loss, we can endure. In waiting, we can be patient. In abundance, we can stay humble. Today, whatever you are facing, this verse is for you. Not as a slogan for success, but as a lifeline of strength. Christ is with you. He will strengthen you for whatever this day holds.
question: What are you facing today that you need Christ's strength to endure with contentment?
prayer: Lord Jesus, I can do all things through You who strengthen me. Teach me contentment in every circumstance, and give me strength for whatever this day holds. Amen.

text: Herein is our love made perfect, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment: because as he is, so are we in this world.
reflection: John writes about a love so complete that it removes fear: "Herein is our love made perfect, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment: because as he is, so are we in this world." When God's love grows to maturity in us, it gives us confidence, even about the day of judgment. Why? Because we are united with Jesus. As He is, so are we. His standing before the Father becomes our standing. That frees us from the fear of punishment. The next verse says perfect love casts out fear. And love made perfect is not only something we receive. It is something we live out. As we love others the way Christ loves us, His love takes deeper root in our lives. Confidence and love grow together. Today, let His perfect love drive out your fears. Then let that same love flow outward in practical action. Show love to someone today, and grow in the confidence of being fully loved by God.
question: What fear could God's perfect love drive out of your heart today?
prayer: Lord, perfect Your love in me so that I may have boldness instead of fear. Let Your love drive out my fears and flow through me in practical acts of love. Amen.

text: (For he that wrought effectually in Peter to the apostleship of the circumcision, the same was mighty in me toward the Gentiles:)
reflection: Paul explains that God worked through both Peter and himself, but in different ways: "For he that wrought effectually in Peter to the apostleship of the circumcision, the same was mighty in me toward the Gentiles." Peter was called mainly to reach Jewish people. Paul was called to reach Gentiles. Their assignments were different, but the same God empowered both. This is a helpful reminder for anyone who compares their calling with others. Your path may look different from someone else's. Your gifts, opportunities, and audience may differ. But the same God who works mightily in others is working in you. Your assignment is not less important because it is different. God does not use everyone in the same way, but He uses everyone who is willing. Today, embrace the calling God has given you. Stop comparing it to someone else's. Trust that He is working effectively in you, just as He did in Peter and Paul, for His purposes and His glory.
question: Whose calling are you comparing yours to, and how can you embrace your own?
prayer: Lord, the same power that worked in Peter and Paul is at work in me. Free me from comparison, and help me embrace the calling You have given me. Amen.

text: But even after that we had suffered before, and were shamefully entreated, as ye know, at Philippi, we were bold in our God to speak unto you the gospel of God with much contention.
reflection: Paul and his companions had been beaten and imprisoned in Philippi. They had every reason to keep quiet when they reached the next city. But Paul writes, "we were bold in our God to speak unto you the gospel of God with much contention." Notice the source of their boldness: bold in our God. Their courage did not come from personality or confidence in themselves. It came from God. And it did not depend on easy circumstances. They spoke with much contention, in the face of opposition. This is courage for today's calling. Most of us will not face prison for our faith. But we do face moments that require courage: speaking up for what is right, sharing our faith, setting boundaries, or doing the hard thing when it would be easier to stay silent. Past hurts can make us hesitate. But Paul shows that courage can rise again. Today, be bold in your God. Ask Him for courage to do what He has called you to do.
question: Where is God calling you to be bold even after past hurts make you hesitate?
prayer: Lord, make me bold in You. When past hurts make me hesitate, let my courage rise again from You, and help me do what You have called me to do. Amen.

text: Give unto the LORD, O ye mighty, give unto the LORD glory and strength.
reflection: Psalm 29 opens with a call to the mighty: "Give unto the LORD, O ye mighty, give unto the LORD glory and strength." The psalmist calls even the powerful ones, perhaps angels, perhaps earthly rulers, to recognize that all glory and strength belong to God. It is an invitation to bow. The rest of the psalm describes God's voice thundering over the waters, breaking cedars, and shaking the wilderness. Compared to His power, every human strength looks small. Yet this psalm ends with a beautiful promise: "The LORD will give strength unto his people." The God who receives all strength also gives strength. When we acknowledge His greatness, we discover that He shares His power with those who trust Him. Today, give God the glory He deserves. Acknowledge that every strength you have comes from Him. And then receive His strength for whatever you face. The God of thunder is also the God who strengthens His people with peace.
question: What strength do you have that you could acknowledge as coming from God?
prayer: Lord, all glory and strength belong to You. I give You the glory You deserve, and I receive Your strength and peace for whatever I face. Amen.

text: He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.
reflection: As we close this month on courage and strength, Isaiah gives a promise for the weary: "He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength." God does not only strengthen the strong. He gives power to the faint, to those who feel they have nothing left. When you are exhausted, discouraged, or overwhelmed, you are exactly the kind of person this promise is for. In the next verses, Isaiah says even young people grow tired, but those who wait on the LORD will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings as eagles, run and not be weary, walk and not faint. Strength is not something we must manufacture. It is something we receive as we wait on God. Today, if you are running on empty, stop and wait on Him. Bring Him your weakness. Rest in His presence. He specializes in giving power to the faint. Let Him renew you for the days ahead.
question: Where are you running on empty, and how can you wait on God for renewed strength?
prayer: Lord, You give power to the faint and increase strength to those who have no might. I bring You my weakness and wait on You. Renew me for the days ahead. Amen.
